extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science and foundational physics (undergraduate/graduate level and general readers interested in concepts of space, time, and motion)
extracted.subtask_short: conceptual analysis of space and time
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpt analyzing space and time as modes of perception and the conceptual tools (conceptual time, kinematics, point-motion, rigid bodies) used to describe motion. Focuses on how scientific concepts function as idealizations and limits drawn in conception to simplify perceptual complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space and Time are modes of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Space and Time are not realities of the phenomenal world, but the modes under which we perceive things apart. They are not infinitely large nor infinitely divisible, but are essentially limited by the contents of our perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that both space and time depend on the association of immediate and stored sense-impressions; they are 'frame' and 'canvas' for perception rather than entities in themselves. Warns against projecting ideal infinities/eternities of conceptual space/time into perceptual reality; gives metaphors (frame/canvas, picture) and consequences for interpreting phenomena and superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual time vs. Conceptual time
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptual time is the perception of sequence in stored sense-impressions (involving memory and consciousness) and has no future or eternal past; conceptual time is an ideal (absolute, uniformly flowing) construct used for description and measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceptual time marks the history of consciousness and is limited by how far stored impressions can be carried back. Conceptual time is likened to ruled paper with equal divisions used to inscribe sequences (past known and predicted future); it is a limit drawn in imagination and invaluable as shorthand, but must not be conflated with perceptual reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of time relies on recurring sense-impressions / astronomical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: We measure time by recurring sense-impressions shown by experience to repeat (e.g., day/night) and by instruments (clocks) regulated ultimately by astronomical motions such as the earth's rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses practical measurement (day/night, clock hands) and the chain of regulation back to astronomical standards (mean solar time, Greenwich). Raises epistemic problems: the earth may not be a perfect timekeeper; comparing different periodic phenomena over long times may not establish absolute uniformity; highlights that measurement conventions rest on empirical regularities, not absolute guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute time is a conceptual ideal unattainable in perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute, true, mathematical time (flowing at a constant rate unaffected by motions of material things) is a pure ideal and cannot be measured in the sphere of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes Newton's definition and argues that 'uniform flow' is a limit drawn from observed approximate sameness; absolute intervals are conceptual means for description and should not be projected into perception. Warns against rhapsodies about eternities based on conceptual divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific concepts are limits drawn in conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific concepts are, as a rule, limits drawn in conception to processes which can be started but not carried to a conclusion in perception (e.g., geometrical surface, atom, ether).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concepts serve as shorthand methods of describing the correlation and sequence of phenomena; they are not asserted to have real existence behind phenomena but are valid as economical descriptive tools. Example: conceptual space and time arise from this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of thought as criterion for conceptual tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of scientific conceptualization includes an 'economy of thought'—concepts enable brief, efficient description and retention of complex perceptual data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links economy of thought to stored sense-impressions and association; treats scientific abstraction as societally useful (analogy to worker-bees) and correlates theoretical power with other brain developments. Suggests economy of thought is allied to an 'economy of energy' in cognitive terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry of Motion / Kinematics as a conceptual mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometry of motion (kinematics) is the conceptual mode in which we classify and describe perceptual change, representing and measuring motion abstractly without reference to particular physical causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its validity depends on the power it gives to resume facts of perception and economize thought rather than absolute correspondence with reality. Applying kinematics to natural types of motion leads to laws of motion and concepts like mass and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-motion as the simplest ideal motion and continuity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion of a point along a curve is the simplest ideal motion used to represent perceptual motion; the series of positions taken up by a point-like element is continuous (no breaks) in normal perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed via limiting processes (man → button → bead → geometrical point). Point-motion captures many temporal features (when starts/stops, faster/slower) but omits many details (rotation, internal limb movements). Emphasizes we cannot perceive true mathematical points; we reach them by conceptual limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of motion types: translation and rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation corresponds to change of position of a body (point-motion); rotation corresponds to change of aspect (orientation) of a rigid body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even for a rigid body, point-motion must be supplemented with rotation description to fully represent motion (e.g., which way the body faces, spinning). These are fundamental idealized categories for describing perceptual motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific definition of a rigid body
rubrics_metrics.description: A body is said to remain rigid during any given motion when the distances between all pairs of its points remain unaltered throughout the whole duration of the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes ideal rigid bodies from real objects (which change shape); notes the need for accurate/scientific definition rather than popular language (table/chair). The rigid-body ideal underlies geometric descriptions of rotation about lines through points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity and eternity are products of conception, not perceptual realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinities of space or eternity of time have no meaning in the field of perception; they are conceptions produced by carrying observed regularities to limits in imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that perceptual experience does not require infinite frames; caution against using conceptual infinities to claim real existence in phenomena. Reiterates that many philosophical/religious confusions stem from conflating conception with perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual modes are individual and deviations are abnormal
rubrics_metrics.description: Space and time are modes carried by each individual's perceptive faculty; if someone's modes differ (e.g., claiming communication beyond ordinary space/time), they have different modes, and persistent deviation classifies as abnormal (ecstatic or insane) unless explained by development or sickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses example of theosophists claiming communication by 'putting aside space and time' to show they refer to their own perceptive modes. Justifies using common experiential regularities to define a 'normal' perceptive faculty and to classify outliers.
